Alika Victor: Building Practical Wellness for Real Life

  • August 3, 2026
  • 11:51 am
  • Cover Story
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:01
Instaread

How a former corporate leader turned wellness expert is helping professionals navigate burnout, uncertainty, and sustainable change through The Practical Wellness Method™

The wellness industry is filled with plans, programs, and promises. New strategies emerge constantly, offering solutions for everything from productivity and stress management to fitness and personal growth. Yet despite the abundance of information available today, many people continue to struggle with creating lasting change.

For Alika Victor, the reason is surprisingly simple.

Most people do not have a knowledge problem. They have a capacity problem.

As the creator of The Practical Wellness Method™, founder of Thrive Now Wellness, author of Becoming Better, and visionary behind WellXchange™, Alika has built her work around helping people close the gap between knowing what is good for them and actually being able to do it consistently.

Drawing from more than a decade of corporate leadership experience and her work as a Board-Certified Health & Wellness Coach, she has developed a practical approach to wellness that resonates with busy professionals, entrepreneurs, caregivers, and parents who are trying to balance demanding responsibilities with their own well-being.

Her mission is not about helping people become perfect. It is about helping them become better, one practical step at a time.

A Lesson Hidden in a Candy Drawer

Alika’s journey into wellness did not begin with a major life event or dramatic transformation. Instead, it started with a simple experiment.

In 2015, she decided to stop replenishing the candy in her desk drawer for one week.

“There was no dramatic overhaul. No strict diet. Just one small change,” she recalls.

That single decision eventually turned into nearly seven years without refined sugar. More importantly, it sparked a deeper understanding of behavior change.

Years later, during a period of intense work demands and competing priorities, she found herself reaching for candy again. Rather than viewing the experience as a failure, she examined it more closely.

“Looking back, I don’t see that as a failure of willpower or resilience,” she says. “I was resilient. I continued showing up and doing what needed to be done. What I lacked was capacity.”

That realization would become one of the defining ideas behind her future work.

Alika recognized that many people blame themselves for struggling with healthy habits when the real issue is often exhaustion, stress, and depleted mental resources. The challenge is not always motivation. Sometimes people simply do not have enough capacity left to support meaningful change.

That insight would eventually become a cornerstone of The Practical Wellness Method™.

Corporate Leadership and the Human Side of Change

Before entering the wellness space full time, Alika spent more than twelve years working in leadership and change-related roles with organizations including CVS Caremark, Conduent, and symplr.

One of the accomplishments she remains most proud of was helping build a Product Management PMO from the ground up at CVS Caremark.

While the work involved strategy, systems, and organizational transformation, it also taught her lessons that would later shape her coaching philosophy.

“What I learned is that even the smartest strategy can fail if you don’t account for the humans expected to execute it,” she explains.

Organizations often devote significant resources to planning, technology, and process improvement. Yet many initiatives fail because leaders underestimate the impact of stress, fatigue, and change on employees.

Alika observed that sustainable transformation depends on more than good ideas. It depends on people’s ability to absorb, adapt, and perform within changing environments.

That lesson applies just as strongly to personal growth as it does to organizational change.

Whether someone is trying to implement a new business strategy or establish healthier habits, success ultimately depends on their capacity to sustain the effort over time.

Creating a Process Instead of a Plan

One of Alika’s most recognizable statements is simple but powerful:

“Most coaching gives you a plan. I give you a process.”

The distinction lies at the heart of her approach.

Many wellness programs assume that people can follow a structured roadmap if they simply stay motivated enough. Alika believes that assumption ignores the realities of everyday life.

Careers become demanding. Family responsibilities shift. Unexpected challenges arise. Stress levels fluctuate.

“A plan assumes life will cooperate. A process assumes it won’t,” she says.

Her background in product management, process improvement, and change management influenced how she approached wellness coaching. Instead of creating another wellness framework focused solely on goals and accountability, she designed a system that could adapt to changing circumstances.

The Practical Wellness Method™ is built around seven principles: Tiny Experiments, Strengths-Centered Growth, Curiosity Over Judgment, the Real-Life Growth Curve, Integrated Wellness, Resilience and Self-Compassion, and Personalization and Adaptability.

At the center of all seven principles is the belief that capacity matters.

The method encourages people to experiment, learn, and adjust rather than striving for perfection. Progress is measured not by flawless execution but by sustainable growth over time.

Alika believes this approach is what allows wellness practices to remain effective even when life becomes complicated.

“People don’t need another overwhelming plan,” she says. “They need a process that works when life doesn’t.”

Navigating the Reality of Modern Work

Today’s workplace presents challenges that previous generations could scarcely have imagined.

Artificial intelligence, organizational restructuring, leadership changes, remote work dynamics, increasing workloads, and shifting priorities have become part of everyday professional life.

For Alika, these issues share a common underlying theme: ambiguity.

“If I had to name one challenge, it would be constant change,” she explains.

Professionals are not only managing their responsibilities. They are also trying to make sense of uncertainty surrounding them.

Alika believes ambiguity has become one of the most significant wellness challenges facing modern workplaces. When people spend large amounts of mental energy trying to understand changing expectations and uncertain circumstances, their capacity begins to erode.

The result is often burnout, disengagement, reduced performance, and chronic stress.

What makes this particularly challenging is that many of the professionals she works with are highly capable and deeply committed individuals.

“They know they should exercise, manage stress, sleep better, and take care of themselves. Knowledge isn’t the issue.”

The issue, she argues, is that work is changing faster than many people can process.

As a result, practical wellness today must extend beyond traditional health advice. It must help people preserve their capacity, maintain resilience, and remain adaptable in environments characterized by constant uncertainty.

Combining Evidence with Compassion

As a Board-Certified Health & Wellness Coach with certifications in behavior change, nutrition, weight management, and group fitness, Alika places significant value on evidence-based practice.

She stays informed about research involving habits, neuroplasticity, self-compassion, and sustainable behavior change.

Yet she is equally committed to recognizing the uniqueness of each individual.

“I think of it as two sides of the same coin,” she says.

Scientific evidence provides valuable guidance, but people do not experience research studies. They experience real life.

Alika believes the emotional side of coaching is where evidence becomes meaningful action. Curiosity replaces judgment. Self-compassion replaces shame. Small experiments replace perfectionism.

While writing her book Becoming Better, she asked friends and colleagues what practical wellness meant to them. Their responses varied widely.

For some, wellness meant movement and fitness. For others, it meant sleep, time outdoors, meaningful relationships, or maintaining independence.

The exercise reinforced a lesson she sees repeatedly in her work: wellness is deeply personal.

There is no universal blueprint for well-being.

The role of coaching is to help people translate evidence into actions that align with their unique circumstances and goals.

Living the Philosophy

Alika’s personal approach to wellness reflects the same principles she teaches.

Rather than following rigid schedules, she structures her days around anchors.

Most mornings begin with a walk before engaging with screens. Throughout the day she intentionally incorporates movement, mindfulness, and recovery practices.

Her work includes coaching, speaking, content creation, program development, caregiver support groups, and growing both Thrive Now Wellness and WellXchange™.

Like many entrepreneurs, she acknowledges that some days are more balanced than others.

Instead of chasing perfection, she focuses on understanding her energy, capacity, and rhythms.

Creative expression also plays an important role in her life. She regularly explores movement and flow artistry, develops movement-based content, and collaborates on creative storytelling projects with photographer Rick Pascale.

For Alika, creativity is not separate from wellness. It is one of the ways she stays engaged, curious, and grounded.

She also finds meaning in simple daily practices, including a gratitude ritual shared with her partner and caring for their two cats.

Since 2019, she has spent time caring for community cats near Arizona State University’s Research Park, an experience that continues to remind her that wellness is often found in small acts of consistency and compassion.

The Future of Practical Wellness

Looking ahead, Alika is particularly excited about the growth of WellXchange™.

The idea emerged from a simple question she began exploring in 2025:

“What if wellness ideas deserved their own stage?”

That question evolved into a platform dedicated to sharing practical wellness ideas from experts, researchers, practitioners, and everyday people.

Alika believes conversations about burnout, caregiving, resilience, loneliness, and workplace stress deserve greater visibility.

Her vision is to create a global exchange where evidence-based wellness ideas can be shared, explored, and adopted in meaningful ways.

Alongside WellXchange™, she continues to expand her speaking engagements and help organizations address burnout, workplace ambiguity, and sustainable performance.

Ultimately, her mission remains grounded in the same philosophy that inspired her work from the beginning.

She wants to help people navigate real life with greater resilience, adaptability, and self-compassion.

In a culture that often celebrates perfection, Alika Victor offers something more practical and far more sustainable. She reminds people that growth does not require flawless execution. It requires curiosity, consistency, and the willingness to keep moving forward.

By helping people protect their capacity and create change that fits the realities of everyday life, she is reshaping the conversation around wellness for a generation that needs practical solutions more than ever.
